paras: The Spanish Camp massacre was the killing of Black residents at Spanish Camp, Wharton County, Texas, early on Sunday, February 26, 1888, when attackers fired a cabin and shot its occupants as they fled. Later reports put the dead at seven of the eight people inside, and the body of a Black man, William Battle, was found hanging nearby. The killings, traced to a land suit the Black residents had won, drew national wire coverage, a Texas editorial dispute over the governor's response, arrests, and mention in the United States Senate.

Spanish Camp lay about sixty miles west of Houston, far from railroads and telegraph lines, and the Houston dispatch described it as "composed of Mexicans, negroes and desperate whites." According to the Fort Worth Daily Gazette's Houston correspondent, a suit over the land on which the Black residents lived had been decided "against some white men" at Wharton about a month before. A summary reprinted by the San Marcos Free Press added that white men who "coveted the ground" had ordered the occupants to leave and that they refused.

The attack came about 2 o'clock on Sunday morning, by the Houston dispatches, or late Saturday night, by the account of Frank Wilson, the Black schoolteacher at Spanish Camp who carried the first news to Houston. Wilson said "unknown persons" poured kerosene around the house and lit it, and men in ambush fired on the occupants as they tried to escape. Five were shot as they rushed out and two, described by Wilson as boys, were shot inside and their bodies burned; one escaped, severely wounded. Nearby, William Battle was found hanging to a tree, thought to have been hanged the same night. The Wharton County sheriff went to the scene with a posse, but no arrests were reported at first.

Governor Ross issued a protest against mob violence that referred to Wharton among other counties, and he sent state rangers to aid the county authorities. Around March 20, two more Black men were reported killed near Spanish Camp on "Battel's plantation," and a Richmond, Texas, dispatch described "a reign of terror" and a secret society believed formed among white planters. On March 29, Sheriff Jones and the rangers arrested three white men under twenty-one, amid a rumor that a Black boy had named thirteen men in the party. Four persons had been arrested by April 11, but no report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Houston wire ran from Washington to Sacramento under headlines such as "Negroes Shot and Burned," "Eight Negroes Murdered in Texas," "Incarnate Fiends" and "Outlaw's Paradise." The Stark County Democrat called it "Deliberate Murder of Eight Inoffensive Negroes," and the Washington Evening Star's telegram summary carried the line "Lynchers Who Had No Compassion." Weekly roundups and condensed-news columns reduced the story to a sentence or two.

In Texas, the San Marcos Free Press contrasted the governor's strong protest against a Panola County lynching with his near silence on Wharton. The San Antonio Daily Light said the governor "coos mildly as a sucking dove" over the Wharton killings and charged the Democratic press with failing to denounce them. Answering the Victoria Advocate, which accused it of exploiting the murders and noted that some of those arrested were "good republicans," the Light said the same journals would have thundered had seven white men been killed by Black men. In August, Senator Chandler cited the "massacre of nine negroes" by "a Wharton County mob" in a Senate speech on the Louisiana election.

The first wire gave five killed outright, one wounded and two burned, later Houston reports said seven killed, and the New York Evening World counted eight by including the hanged man. Late-March dispatches spoke of six dead, and Chandler of nine on a date he gave as February 28, 1885. Battle's link rests on the wire's "it is thought," and the later Houston tallies of seven dead do not include him.

accounts.label: Houston wire (first report)
accounts.gist: A negro cabin was fired Sunday morning and the occupants shot as they ran; five killed outright, one wounded, two consumed; William Battle found hanged nearby; attributed to a land suit won by the negroes.

accounts.label: Frank Wilson, Black schoolteacher
accounts.gist: Unknown persons poured kerosene around the house late Saturday night and fired from ambush on the occupants; some were killed in the yard and two boys were shot inside and left to burn.

accounts.label: Later Houston special
accounts.gist: Seven killed, not five, and one severely wounded; five shot as they rushed out and two shot inside and their bodies cremated; the suit had been decided against some white men.

accounts.label: Exchange summary (San Marcos Free Press)
accounts.gist: White men who coveted the land ordered the Black occupants to vacate, lost in court, then gathered an armed party, fired the house with eight asleep inside, and killed seven.

accounts.label: Senator Chandler
accounts.gist: Nine men, driven one by one from a house the court had adjudged theirs, were shot to death by a Wharton County mob.

framing.detail: The Houston wire called it 'perhaps the most horrible crime' in that section, and headlines read 'Wholesale Butchery', 'Deliberate Murder of Eight Inoffensive Negroes' and 'Shocking Butchery'.
Other papers ran the wire under headlines such as 'Incarnate Fiends', 'Outlaw's Paradise' and 'Negroes Burned Out and Shot Down', or reduced it to a line in news roundups.

The San Marcos Free Press and San Antonio Daily Light faulted the governor for denouncing the Panola lynching while barely mentioning Wharton, and the Light charged the Democratic press with silence because the victims were Black.
The Victoria Advocate, as quoted, accused the Light of exploiting the murders for politics and noted that some of those arrested were Republicans.

versions.value: Five killed outright, one wounded, two consumed (seven dead in cabin)

conflicts.note: The first and later Houston reports are compatible (five shot outside plus two inside); the fuller Houston special of Feb. 29 (A6) explicitly corrects 'five' to seven killed. 'Six' appears only in late-March summaries and 'nine' in a Senate speech months later.
The Memphis Appeal's wire copy (A9) gives 'about 3 o'clock'. Chandler's year is plainly wrong against the contemporaneous reports.
